summary: Describes the Neighborhood Discovery Protocol for mobile ad hoc networks, which lets a node learn its one-hop and symmetric two-hop neighbors. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: NHDP lets routers in a mobile ad hoc network learn which neighboring routers they can hear and which links work in both directions. It shares that local information with routing protocols that need to choose paths or reduce network-wide message forwarding.

questions: how does manet neighbor discovery work
what is the nhdp hello message
subtitle: How mobile ad hoc routers discover direct links and symmetric neighbors two hops away.

tldr.problem: Mobile ad hoc routers need current connectivity information even when wireless links are lossy, one-way, and changing quickly.
tldr.mechanism: Each MANET interface exchanges HELLO messages that advertise local addresses and link status. Routers use the reports to update their one-hop links and symmetric two-hop neighbor information.
tldr.outcome: NHDP stores this information in protocol information bases for other MANET protocols to use. RFC 6130 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 7183, RFC 7188, and RFC 7466.

today: RFC 6130 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2011. It has been updated by RFC 7183, RFC 7188, and RFC 7466.

sections.title: Why Neighborhood Discovery Is Needed
sections.content:
The Neighborhood Discovery Protocol (NHDP) lets each mobile ad hoc network (MANET) router identify its one-hop neighbors and its symmetric two-hop neighbors. Routers exchange HELLO messages using the packet and message format in RFC 5444. Other MANET protocols can read the resulting local connectivity information.

Wireless reception is not necessarily two-way: one router may hear another without the reverse being true. Links and network membership can change quickly, and one router may have multiple interfaces on different channels. NHDP tracks these changes without a central controller.
sections.plainLanguage: NHDP gives each router current information about nearby routers and links. It is designed for networks where wireless messages can be lost and devices can move.

sections.title: Heard Links and Symmetric Neighbors
sections.content:
A router considers an interface heard when it can receive control messages from that interface. A link exists if either end can hear the other, while a symmetric link exists only if both ends can hear each other. A one-hop neighbor is a router whose interface is heard; a symmetric two-hop neighbor is a symmetric one-hop neighbor of one of this router's symmetric one-hop neighbors.

A router must have at least one MANET interface. Each interface has one or more network addresses, which must be unique to the router and must not overlap addresses assigned to another router in the same reachable network.
sections.plainLanguage: One router hearing another does not prove that both can exchange messages. NHDP calls a link symmetric only after it has evidence of communication in both directions.

sections.title: The Information Bases
sections.content:
NHDP keeps local state in information bases. The Local Information Base records the router's interfaces and recently removed addresses. Each MANET interface has an Interface Information Base with a Link Set and a 2-Hop Set. The Neighbor Information Base records current and recently lost one-hop neighbors.

Link tuples track neighbor interface addresses, heard and symmetric expiration times, link quality, and status. A tuple may be pending, lost, symmetric, or heard. Expired information is removed so other protocols can use a current view of the neighborhood.
sections.plainLanguage: NHDP keeps one set of records about the router, one for each MANET interface, and one about its neighbors. Expiration times prevent old reports from being treated as current.

sections.title: HELLO Messages and Address Status
sections.content:
NHDP defines one message type: HELLO. HELLO messages are local and must not be forwarded; if a message hop limit is present, it must be one. Each HELLO contains exactly one VALIDITY_TIME message TLV to state how long its information remains valid. Periodic HELLO messages should also contain an INTERVAL_TIME TLV.

Address Block TLVs identify the sender's own interface addresses with LOCAL_IF, report neighbor-link status with LINK_STATUS, and list other symmetric neighbors with OTHER_NEIGHB. A receiver uses these fields to distinguish heard, symmetric, and lost links.
sections.plainLanguage: A HELLO message announces the sender's interfaces and reports what it knows about nearby links. A validity field tells other routers how long to keep that information.

sections.title: Sending and Processing HELLO Messages
sections.content:
Each MANET interface generates HELLO messages according to its own parameters. A router may send them periodically, after a change, or both. If it sends periodic HELLOs, each new message must be sent within HELLO_INTERVAL, and successive messages must respect HELLO_MIN_INTERVAL. Jitter should be used unless the medium already prevents simultaneous interfering transmissions.

On receipt, a router discards invalid HELLO messages without processing them. Valid messages update the Neighbor Set, Lost Neighbor Set, Link Sets, and 2-Hop Sets. A link becomes symmetric when the neighbor's HELLO reports the receiver's address as heard or symmetric; only then does the receiver record the sender's other reported neighbors as symmetric two-hop neighbors.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers send HELLO messages on their participating interfaces and refresh the reported neighbor information regularly. A router treats a link as two-way only when the reports show that both sides can hear each other.

sections.title: Using Local Link Quality
sections.content:
An implementation may track link quality as a value from zero to one, where a larger value means a better link. The value is local to the router and is not included in HELLO signaling. Routers therefore can interoperate even when they use different link-quality methods or do not use link quality.

Link quality is an admission check, not a routing metric. The HYST_ACCEPT and HYST_REJECT thresholds let a router accept a link above one threshold and reject it below another, keeping its status unchanged between them.
sections.plainLanguage: A router may avoid links whose quality is too low. Separate accept and reject thresholds reduce rapid status changes when quality moves around a boundary.

sections.title: Security of HELLO Information
sections.content:
A correctly formatted HELLO can still contain false information about the sender's addresses, link states, or neighbors. Other routers may record that information, and the effects depend on the routing protocol that uses it. NHDP's processing rules maintain consistent information-base contents but cannot establish that every report is truthful.

The RFC does not require one security method for all networks. Physical access controls or link-layer protection may be sufficient in some settings. Where needed, a security protocol can add a cryptographic signature to a message or packet; a HELLO that fails signature verification should be rejected without processing.
sections.plainLanguage: A router can send a validly formed but false neighbor report. Networks can use link-layer security or signed messages, depending on the protection they need.

items.title: Local Information Base
items.text: Records the router's interfaces and recently removed addresses.

items.title: Interface Information Base
items.text: One per MANET interface, with links and symmetric two-hop neighbors.

items.title: Neighbor Information Base
items.text: Records current and recently lost one-hop neighbors.
